idea.raw_idea: Owners constantly ask how they would know if they can afford a second location. After twelve years doing books for dental practices, the answer is never about projected production at the new site. It is about whether your first location generates enough collected cash to survive the financing drag of the second.
idea.angle: You can afford a second location only when your first location stays cash-positive while carrying the financing weight of the new one for two quarters.
idea.why: DSOs keep acquiring independent offices, pushing owners to consider a second location to stay competitive. Simultaneously, equipment financing demand is climbing. Owners need a concrete framework to evaluate this move without guessing.
idea.signal: DSOs keep buying independent practices

verdict.memory_quote: Equipment financing looks cheap monthly but practices that financed more than two major items in a year were cash-negative for the next two quarters.

verdict.note: Uses specific financing observation from author’s experience.

idea.raw_idea: An owner thought hiring a new hygienist was out of the question because the bank balance was too low. The real cost of waiting was not just lost appointments. It was running the schedule short while insurance reimbursements sat uncollected for weeks, which meant the practice bled capacity it could not get back.
idea.angle: Delaying a hire because your bank balance looks thin often costs more than the salary, especially when the missing cash is stuck in an insurance lag you have not measured.
idea.why: Hygienist wages are rising due to shortages, making owners even more hesitant to hire. At the same time, insurers are slowing reimbursements. This creates a paralyzing squeeze where owners misread their own cash position and delay necessary hires.
idea.signal: Hygienist shortage drives wages up

idea.why: Equipment financing demand is climbing among small businesses, and steady loan rates make the monthly payments look deceptively manageable. Owners need a hard rule before they sign.

idea.raw_idea: Distributors are raising prices on consumables, but the real cost of inaction is not the price hike itself. It is running your practice assuming supplies are five percent of revenue when our work consistently shows they sit closer to eight percent, which means every month you delay updating your numbers, you are planning your spending around three percent of revenue that is already gone.
idea.angle: If you still estimate your supply costs at five percent of revenue while distributors raise prices, you are making every other financial decision in the practice based on money that is already spent.
idea.why: Distributors just announced price increases on consumables, making supply costs a timely anxiety. But the author's verified experience shows the deeper problem is the baseline guess owners use, which makes this response unique to Ledgerline.
idea.signal: Supply costs rise for dental offices
